w: Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar broke ground on Sabika hill in 1238, and Nasrid rulers spent two centuries perfecting it. After 1492 it became Ferdinand and Isabella's royal court, where Columbus secured backing for his voyage. Napoleon's troops later blew holes in the walls before British travellers rediscovered the ruins.
s: A hilltop fortress two centuries and two faiths in the making
_facts: Begun 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar
Became royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella after 1492
Columbus received royal backing for his voyage here
Napoleon's troops damaged it in 1812

w: The Nasrid rulers' summer palace and country estate, built directly uphill from the Alhambra so the court could retreat there without ever leaving the hill -- a quieter, private counterpart to the fortress next door.
s: The Nasrid summer retreat next door to the Alhambra
_facts: Summer palace and country estate of the Nasrid rulers
Located directly east of and uphill from the Alhambra

w: North of the Darro River, the Albaicin has kept its medieval street plan intact since the Nasrid period -- the same tangle of alleys the last Muslim rulers of Spain walked before 1492. In 1994 UNESCO folded the whole quarter into the Alhambra's World Heritage listing.
s: Granada's Nasrid street plan, still tangled after 700 years
_facts: Retains its medieval Nasrid-period street plan (13th-15th c.)
North of the Darro river
Declared World Heritage Site in 1994 as extension of the Alhambra

w: Charles V ordered a Renaissance palace built inside his Nasrid inheritance in 1527 -- construction stalled after 1637, and the building sat roofless for three centuries. It was never once slept in by a monarch. Leopoldo Torres Balbas restored it after 1923; the roof went on in 1967. Now it just houses two museums.
s: A Renaissance palace that stood roofless for 300 years
_facts: Construction began 1527, unfinished after 1637
Never served as a monarch's residence
Stood roofless until 1967
Now houses the Alhambra Museum and Fine Arts Museum

w: The Garcia Lorca family's summer home from 1926 to 1936, where Federico wrote many of his most important works. In August 1936, with Francoist soldiers closing in, he fled here one last time before leaving for good. The house and its orchards now form the park that carries his name, opened in 1995.
s: Where Lorca wrote, then fled Francoist soldiers in 1936
_facts: Garcia Lorca family's summer home, 1926-1936
He fled here pursued by Francoist soldiers in August 1936
Now the heart of Parque Federico Garcia Lorca, opened 1995

w: Granada's Romani settled this hillside opposite the Alhambra after the 1492 Reconquista, carving homes into the whitewashed caves that still riddle the slope. They speak Calo, a language rooted in India that's fading fast. Federico Garcia Lorca immortalised the community in his Romancero Gitano.
s: Granada's Romani quarter, carved into whitewashed caves
_facts: Traditional neighbourhood of the Granadian Romani since 1492
Cave houses in whitewashed caves
Romani speak Calo, derived from India, now declining
Portrayed by Lorca in Romancero Gitano

w: Tucked inside the Alhambra, the Partal Palace is the oldest surviving palatial structure on the site -- built in the early 14th century by the Nasrid ruler Muhammad III, decades before Yusuf I and Muhammad V's more famous additions went up around it.
s: The oldest palace inside the Alhambra
_facts: Built in the early 14th century by Muhammad III
Oldest surviving palatial structure in the Alhambra

w: Once Bab Ilbira in Arabic, this gate started as part of Granada's 11th-century Zirid walls before being rebuilt into a fortified checkpoint in the 14th century. Only a fragment survives today, at the edge of the Albaicin. Outside its arch once lay the Ibn Malik Cemetery, a vast Muslim burial ground.
s: A fragment of Granada's 11th-century Zirid walls
_facts: Originally part of the 11th-century Zirid walls
Rebuilt into a fortified gate in the 14th century
The Ibn Malik Muslim cemetery once stood outside it
Only part of the gate remains today

w: Granada's archaeological collection has lived since the 20th century inside the Castril Palace, a 16th-century Renaissance house on the Carrera del Darro with a facade dated 1593. The museum itself is older than the building it borrows -- founded in 1879, decades before it found this palatial home.
_facts: Established 1879
Housed in the 16th-century Castril Palace since the 20th century
Facade dated 1593, with a Renaissance patio

w: A Nasrid palace inside the Alhambra that the Spanish conquerors handed to Franciscan friars, who ran it as a convent for centuries. By the early 1900s it had crumbled into ruin; Leopoldo Torres Balbas rebuilt it in the 1920s. Since 1945 it's been a state-run Parador hotel.
s: A Nasrid palace, then a convent, now a hotel
_facts: Former medieval Nasrid palace, converted to a Franciscan convent
Fell into ruin, restored by Torres Balbas in the 1920s
A state-owned Parador hotel since 1945

w: The gateway where the climb to the Alhambra officially begins -- from Plaza Nueva, up the Cuesta de Gomerez, through the Forest of the Alhambra and in through this arch. Every visitor on foot still follows the same route carved out centuries ago.
s: Where the walk up to the Alhambra begins
_facts: Marks the start of the path up to the Alhambra
Path runs from Plaza Nueva up the Cuesta de Gomerez

w: Seventy thousand square metres of science-centre sprawl, with a planetarium, a library, cinemas and -- less expected -- a plastination lab where the museum preserves its own specimens. It belongs to the European Network of Science Centers and Museums, a rare Granada landmark with nothing medieval about it.
s: A science museum with its own plastination lab
_facts: 70,000 square metres, member of ECSITE
Has a planetarium and a plastination lab
Runs restoration and production workshops

w: A small private museum tucked into an ordinary house in the Realejo, Granada's Jewish quarter until the 1492 expulsion. It rebuilds the culture, traditions and daily life of the city's Sephardic community -- one room at a time, in the neighbourhood they were forced to leave.
s: Sephardic life, rebuilt room by room in the old Jewish quarter
_facts: Officially the Jewish Quarter Museum (Museo de la Juderia)
Private initiative in a house in the Realejo
Realejo was Granada's Jewish quarter until the 1492 expulsion
